where: Exam traps, fourth trap (screen size vs distance)
problem: The trap states the rule correctly (use distance to the bounding-sphere centre) but then draws the wrong conclusion from it. With the centre rule the projected size is under-estimated, so a long object loses detail too early, not too late. Staying at high detail far too long is what happens when you use the distance to the nearest vertex. As written, a student will attach the effect to the wrong method and learn the opposite lesson.
fix: Screen size uses the distance to the bounding-sphere centre, not the nearest vertex. Measuring to the nearest vertex over-estimates the projected size, so a long object stays at high detail far too long. The centre rule errs the other way: a long object may drop to a coarse level slightly early, which shows as a pop, so pad the radius.

problem: "The view frustum is the six-sided pyramid of space the camera can see" is loose: a frustum is a pyramid with its top cut off, bounded by six planes. A pyramid has five faces, so "six-sided pyramid" reads as a hexagonal-based pyramid.
fix: The view frustum is the volume the camera can see. It is a pyramid with its top cut off, bounded by six planes: near, far, left, right, top and bottom.

problem: "This is chunked LOD, also called geomipmapping" treats two separately published terrain schemes as one name. Chunked LOD is the quadtree of chunks with per-chunk meshes; geomipmapping is a fixed grid of square patches, each with a few discrete levels and stitched edges. The two are related, not synonyms.
fix: This quadtree terrain scheme is a form of chunked LOD. Geomipmapping is a related scheme: a fixed grid of square patches, each patch drawn at one of a few discrete levels, with neighbouring patch edges stitched so no cracks appear.

problem: The node reads 'LOD 40%' with the note '1,000 tris each', but after LOD each object has 400 triangles. 1,500 objects at 1,000 triangles each would be 1,500,000 triangles, not the 600,000 shown at the end of the flow.
fix: Note on the LOD node: '400 tris each after LOD (1,000 before)'. Then 1,500 × 400 = 600,000 triangles, matching the final node.

problem: "A triangle whose vertices wind clockwise on screen is a back face" is only true under a stated convention. If front faces are counter-clockwise (the usual OpenGL default) the statement holds; Direct3D defaults to clockwise front faces, and then it is wrong.
fix: Take front faces as counter-clockwise on screen, the usual OpenGL convention. A triangle that winds clockwise on screen is then a back face. The convention is set by the graphics API, so state it before using the rule.

problem: "how many pixels a bounding box actually wrote" is imprecise: during an occlusion query the box writes no colour. The query counts fragments or samples that pass the depth test.
fix: hardware occlusion queries that ask the GPU how many samples of a bounding box would pass the depth test, that is, how much of it is actually visible

where: Exam traps, third trap (occlusion culling outdoors)
problem: "An outdoor scene gets no gain from it" is overstated. Terrains have real occluders: hills, buildings, walls, trees. Also a wire fence does occlude partially; the point is that it rarely hides a whole object.
fix: Occlusion culling needs an occluder that is solid and large enough to hide whole objects. Open sky hides nothing and a wire fence hides almost nothing, so flat desert ground gains little. Hills, buildings and walls are real occluders, so outdoor scenes do gain from it.

problem: Listing "backface during rasterisation, then frustum per object" as the cheap-first order confuses cost order with pipeline order: per-object frustum culling has to happen before the object is rasterised at all, since backface culling needs the triangles already in front of the rasteriser.
fix: Do per-object frustum culling on the CPU first, before submitting anything to be drawn. Backface culling then costs nothing extra because the hardware does it during rasterisation. Issue occlusion queries last, because each one costs a round trip to the GPU.
